climbing_route.label: Scramble from the Himmelhorn-Ottohorn col
climbing_route.notes: From the col the summit is reported as easy scrambling — accounts consistently call the peak class 3 and describe it as one of the few Southern Picket summits that is not fifth class. Parties have climbed it from the col in roughly an hour round trip, some without taking rope or rack out of camp. Picket rock is broken and the col itself is loose, so helmets and careful block-testing matter more than the grade suggests; the col is also the retreat point, and getting back down its north side late in the season can be harder than the scramble above.

climbing_route.label: Rockfall scar below the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: At least one party found the easy line broke into a fresh rockfall zone about 30 ft below the summit ridge and backed off rather than cross it, returning with a rope and climbing a roped alternative of about two pitches of juggy 5.7 to the top. Treat this as conditions-dependent rather than fixed: the scar is recent enough that the terrain here may have changed again, and a scramble party arriving without gear may find no acceptable line through the unstable blocks. Carry enough to retreat or to protect a short 5th-class variation, and do not commit to the last 100 ft until you can see it.

climbing_route.label: Snow finger off the Overcoat Glacier
climbing_route.notes: A steep snow finger rises off the glacier toward the summit rock and is the feature the route is known for. It starts as a low-angle ramp and steepens continuously, and parties have wanted a second tool near the top; crevasses cut across it partway up and are the main hazard on this section. In late season the transition from glacier ice to the snow finger and again from snow to rock opens into moats, so expect the exit onto rock to be the awkward part of the day.

climbing_route.label: Heathery slot to the notch
climbing_route.notes: Leave the snow and round the corner onto rock, then scramble a reddish, heather-filled slot set against the mountainside for roughly two thirds of its length before stepping out left (west) onto exposed rock. Route-finding here is the trap on the peak: the obvious south-to-north angled gully that looks like it leads straight to the summit blocks is not the route, and parties who follow it end up under steep, unclimbable terrain. Holds in the correct line are reported solid, but the position is exposed.

climbing_route.label: Angled chimney to the saddle
climbing_route.notes: An angled chimney — overhanging wall on the left above slabby rock on the right — leads to the saddle between the south peak and the true summit. This is stemming and opposition on friction rather than crack climbing, so dry boots and hands make a real difference and it is markedly harder wet. A rope and harnesses already carried for the glacier are worth using here; parties describe it as the section where an inexperienced scrambler gets into trouble.

climbing_route.label: Summit block
climbing_route.notes: The final block stands roughly 400 vertical ft above the surrounding terrain and is steep on every side, so at least class 4 and arguably low 5th is unavoidable to reach the top. Climb the steep gully above the saddle on generally good holds with a few exposed moves over tall steps to gain a roomy summit. Summit rocks have been described as wobbly — test everything, and be aware that anyone below is directly in the fall line. Descent is normally a downclimb through a dihedral and heather ledges followed by two full-length rappels back to the glacier, so bring enough rope and slings to build anchors.

climbing_route.label: Dike shield face pitch
climbing_route.notes: Start in a clean dihedral just left of the dike-streaked shield, roughly 20 ft above the snow — the bergschrund/moat at the base determines whether that start is even reachable and is the first thing to assess. Tiptoe rightward across parallel dikes for about 40 ft to the very edge of the face, then face-climb past an overlap. That dike traverse is the crux and takes essentially no gear for its full length, so a fall here is long; cracks higher on the pitch accept protection. Reported at 55-60 m.

climbing_route.label: Corner system with roof
climbing_route.notes: A clean, well-featured corner system with a small roof near mid-height. In contrast to the first pitch this one protects readily with a standard rack, and it is the most secure climbing on the lower face. Around 60 m.

climbing_route.label: Traverse left to the top of the lower face
climbing_route.notes: Climb up about 10 m, then traverse left around two corners to find the weakness that breaks through the top of the steep lower face and lands on a large ledge. The traverse is the route-finding key on the lower wall — the direct line above does not go — and it puts the second in a swinging-fall position, so consider protecting it for the follower. From the ledge a rock gully leads right toward the ridge crest.

climbing_route.label: Upper ridge crest to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Roughly 270 m of mostly low fifth class along a wide trough in the centre of the face, then out right onto a sharp buttress crest to the summit. The first ascent simul-climbed this and cut below the gendarmes rather than climbing over them to save time, which is worth copying — the whole objective is a long way from anywhere and daylight is the real constraint. Overall grade IV 5.9. Descent is not back down the face: continue along the connecting ridge to Mount Challenger's summit (easy fifth, simul-climbed or belayed) and descend Challenger's normal route over the glacier, so plan for a full traverse and carry glacier gear over the top.

climbing_route.label: Loose gully above Libby Lake
climbing_route.notes: From the south end of Libby Lake two gullies are visible; take the narrower right-hand one. This gully is the one genuinely unpleasant part of the climb — it is consistently described as very loose scree and choss, notably worse than the rock anywhere else in the Sawtooth, and it is the reason to wear a helmet and to avoid climbing directly above or below anyone else in your party. Spread out sideways rather than stacking up.

climbing_route.label: Exit left onto the rib
climbing_route.notes: At about 8,200 ft climb out of the gully to the left onto the rib, where the rock is appreciably more solid, and follow it to the ridge crest at roughly 8,473 ft. Staying in the gully to its top is the common mistake; the rib is both safer and faster. Grade is easy scrambling, class 2+ at most.

climbing_route.label: Ridge traverse to the east summit
climbing_route.notes: Traverse east along the south side of the crest for about half a mile of straightforward class 2-3 scrambling. Several false summits appear along the way — the true high point is the eastern one at roughly 8,572 ft, and reaching it requires dropping to a saddle near 8,380 ft before the final rise. The ridge is high and exposed to weather, and parties have been caught by wind and snow flurries here even in early autumn.

climbing_route.label: Way trail through forest above the pass
climbing_route.notes: This is not a technical climb — above Fourth of July Pass the summit is reached by an abandoned, unmaintained way trail, and the difficulty is navigation and fitness rather than climbing. The path leaves the main trail on its north side near a distinctive tall broken stump marked with old flagging, then traverses northeast on an easy grade through deep mossy forest for half a mile or more. Old flagging is the only marking and it is not reliable; deadfall crosses the tread in places.

climbing_route.label: Rocky rib to the ridge
climbing_route.notes: Between roughly 3,900 and 4,950 ft the tread is lost in a jackstraw blowdown area. The route goes essentially straight uphill through steep but open forest and then up a rocky rib; a cairn and flagging mark where the path resumes near 4,950 ft. This is the section where parties lose the route, so keep a GPS track or note the re-entry point on the way up for the descent.

climbing_route.label: Heather benches and summit slopes
climbing_route.notes: Above 4,950 ft the path switchbacks north through sparse forest on the south ridge, then makes a long leftward traverse across grassy benches and moderate heather, then up a steep southwest-facing heather slope on tight switchbacks. Above about 6,600 ft it becomes scree and talus and the ridge opens out — wide enough that it can be walked without a trail to the gentle summit ridge near 7,400 ft. Steep heather is slick when wet or frosted and holds snow late; snow on these slopes turns a walk-up into a self-arrest problem, so carry an axe outside of high summer.

climbing_route.label: Open slope and gully above the saddle
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle where the maintained trail ends, the summit is about a quarter mile of scrambling. The described line goes up and left, then descends left across an open slope to reach a gully, which is then climbed. The saddle and the slopes on either side are narrow, uneven and cliffed on both sides, and snow lingers here with cornices along the edges into June — an unroped slip on frozen morning snow is the realistic accident on this peak, not a fall while rock climbing.

climbing_route.label: Exposed traverse and summit scramble
climbing_route.notes: Above the gully a short but exposed step right crosses to the summit side; turn back west/left for the final scramble to the 5,958 ft top. The rock work is brief and no harder than class 3, but the exposure is real and the consequence of a fall is fatal, so this is a scramble for people already comfortable moving unroped on exposed terrain. Verify conditions before committing — the same moves are a different proposition with wet rock or old snow in the gully.

climbing_route.label: Notch to the ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: From the notch at the top of the approach gully, skirt the ridge on climber's right over large blocks, then take a dihedral for a couple of moves back up to the crest and belay. The granite here is solid — the tower is regarded as some of the best rock in the state — and the pitch protects well with a light alpine rack. The blocks at the start are the loosest thing on the route and sit directly above anyone still in the gully.

climbing_route.label: Exposed crest pitch
climbing_route.notes: The crux, following the ridge proper on clean rock with good gear. Sources split on the grade: the route is often given 5.0 overall but this pitch is commonly felt to be nearer 5.4, largely because of how exposed it is rather than how hard the moves are. A weakness slightly left of the crest offers the same difficulty with less air under your feet if the position is unwelcome.

climbing_route.label: Upper crest to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Scramble at or just right of the crest to the summit on continued solid rock. Exposure increases toward the top while the climbing eases. Descent reverses the route with some downclimbing plus several rappels; fixed tat and rings exist at various stances but are of unknown age and blocky terrain means anchor choice matters — a 2005 accident on this peak involved a rappel anchor failure after a party had already committed to the wrong gully on approach, so build or back up your own anchors rather than trusting what is there.

climbing_route.label: Glacier exit onto the east rock
climbing_route.notes: Head southwest across the glacier toward the obvious corner where the left skyline of the summit massif meets the east ridge, staying high and right on the glacier and then angling left to within about 100 ft of the east rock face. The face above sheds rock, so move left if debris is coming down and do not linger under it. Leaving the snow for rock near 7,100 ft is where the route gets awkward late in the season — the moat opens and crevasses lower on the slope may force a detour to a lower crossing. Glacier gear can be left at this transition.

climbing_route.label: Heather shelf across the south face
climbing_route.notes: The corkscrew itself: a rock-and-heather shelf carrying a well-worn goat and climber path that cuts high across the entire south face, around the corner and partway onto the west face. The tread is good and the scrambling easy, but above roughly 7,200 ft the ledge is edged by a drop of around 500 ft, so this is the section where a slip is not survivable despite the modest grade. Wet or frosted heather and lingering snow patches on the shelf are the thing to watch.

climbing_route.label: Summit gully to the ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: A prominent gully at the far end of the traverse is climbed straight up to its top at the ridge crest. Mostly second and third class with a few sections where hands are needed; loose material in the gully means keeping the party close together or spread out sideways.

climbing_route.label: Class 4 step and summit scramble
climbing_route.notes: At the crest move east (left) just below the ridge, climb a short steep step of about class 4, then scramble a further 200-300 ft of exposed third class on granite to the summit. Descent reverses the whole line, and the corkscrew is easy to lose from above — note where the shelf leaves the ridge on the way up, because dropping off the wrong side of the south face leads into cliffs.
